title: Chapter 82 – Medicine Valley
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Feng]

Feng counts the silences as he walks, because it is better than counting steps.

The first is the road. It runs up the cleft between black pines, a pale ribbon under a hand of snow, and not a single track marks it. The second is the stream, which should be loud with melt, and runs instead in a thin glassy trickle that makes no noise at all. The third is the sky. There are no crows in it. There is no wind. The whole of Medicine Valley is held, in the blue light before sunrise, like a breath someone has forgotten to let go.

Nine days, Overseer Han said. The beasts have been going up the mountain.

He shifts the sword on his back and keeps his weight on the good leg.

He is twenty-seven. He has been the first-ranker of the Outer Court for two years, and for two years he has known precisely what to do on every road he walked: where to put his feet, whom to watch, when to speak. It is a skill he is proud of. It is also, he is beginning to see, a skill for roads that stay the shape they are.

Ahead of him, at the head of the file, Tan Ruyan walks with her white spear low. Behind her goes Zhao Yao, with his too-big pack. Behind Zhao Yao goes the Inner Sect disciple, Wei Chen, in his indigo hood. And behind them all, last, with a bone-handled satchel on his shoulder and a stick in his hand, walks Feng's brother.

Feng does not look back. He has not looked back for an hour. He knows exactly where the boy is: eleven paces behind, left of the track, careful of his feet.

He has been careful of his feet for a month.

* * *

The array on Terrace Eleven opens at dawn with a sound like a held note.

They stand before the black stone arch and watch the band of yellow light fade from its crown. Two guards in blue unbar the gate. The slope beyond is steeper than it looked from the road, a bank of black earth terraced into three shelves, fenced in iron and crowded with red-leafed plants no higher than a knee. The air above them shimmers. A slow heavy sweetness comes down the slope and catches in the back of Feng's throat.

"Earthheart," says Wei Chen, softly. "Four hundred years."

Feng has never seen a Level 2 herb. He has seen their price, in the Pill Hall, in the column that said restricted. It is different to stand in front of one. The plants do not look like much. But the old pull of the earth is in them, a patient stillness, a feeling that the air itself is leaning in to listen.

Foundation. This is what it is made of.

"Leader," says Wei Chen.

Tan Ruyan steps forward. She plants the butt of her spear in the snow and bows to the terrace, once, from the waist, as to an elder. Then she kneels beside the nearest plant and presses her palm flat to the earth. A pale yellow light spreads from her hand into the soil. It is Earth Qi, and her control of it is beautiful: slow, even, deliberate. The black dirt around the root loosens and sifts aside like water.

"Nine layers of patience," she says, to the plant, almost under her breath. "Come up, then."

Feng, who knows what it costs to cast slowly and cleanly at the eighth layer, watches with grudging respect. She does not hurry. She does not strain. She has not a hair out of place.

She is better than the Court thinks.

The root rises. It is the size of a man's fist, a dull russet knob wrapped in fine red fibers, and it sits in a cradle of loosened earth with the unhurried dignity of a thing that has been waiting thirty years. Tan Ruyan sits back on her heels.

"Pill Hall," she says.

Jian steps up.

He kneels at the edge of the hole. He has the bone tongs in his hands, and he draws them out of the cloth with a curious slow tenderness that Feng recognizes, from the forge: the care of a man who has been given something he does not own. He closes the jaws over the root, a hand's breadth below the crown. He lifts.

It comes free with a sound like a kiss.

Not a fiber is torn. The boy lays it in a bed of dry moss, in the satchel's inner pocket, and wraps it with a hand that does not shake. He does the same with the second. By the time he has finished, the sun is clearing the eastern ridge, and the terrace is gold, and two small dark holes in the soil are all that remain.

"Two," says Wei Chen. "As the Overseer permitted." He looks at the boy with something that might be approval. "You do that well."

"I have been practicing, Senior Brother."

"On what?"

"On pills," says Jian. "It is much the same."

Feng turns his head so that no one can see his face.

It is not the same, he thinks. I have watched him at the Pill Hall. He holds a furnace like a man holding a baby bird. And he is holding this one the same way, with his eyes half shut and his head a little to the side, as if he were listening.

Listening to what?

* * *

Zhao Yao sees the pangolin at the second terrace.

Feng is looking at the wrong thing when it happens. The party has stopped for water on a shelf of rock, a flat stone hip over the stream. Tan Ruyan has gone to the edge to scout the upper valley. Wei Chen sits with his bamboo case across his knee. Jian has taken a half step into the trees, to be sick, he says, and Feng has let him.

There is a rustle.

It is very small. It is the sound of a bag being undone. Feng turns his head in time to see a small bronze-scaled shape go up the trunk of a pine with the unhurried deliberateness of a creature that has been told to stay and has decided not to. It is the length of a forearm. It has a long tail and a short snout. It stops on a branch at the height of a man's head and puts its nose in the air.

Zhao Yao, by the fire, has risen to his feet.

The boy is fourteen and wears the careful stillness of the Zhao house like a borrowed cloak. He does not cry out. He does not reach for the spear. He stands with his hands at his sides and his face white, looking at the creature in the tree, and in his eyes there is nothing at all of surprise.

He knew.

It is an odd thing to see. A boy who has been told a secret and is now being shown it. Feng's gaze goes from the pangolin to the boy, and back, and a cold small piece of understanding turns over in his chest: Jian told him. Or he found out. And he said nothing, not to Tan, not to Wei Chen, not even to me.

So. He trusts him.

It is not jealousy. It is something quieter, a little sore, like pressing a bruise. Feng has been the one his brother trusted for twenty-one years. It is strange to find the list growing.

"A seamwalker," says Zhao Yao, very softly. "A real one."

"Registered," says Feng. He keeps his voice even and rises, casually, putting himself between the boy and the fire. "At the Beast Hall. The keeper has the paper. It came from our hill. It is a pet."

"A pet."

"The Court allows one beast to an apprentice of the Pill Hall." He meets Zhao Yao's eyes. "It was written in the Register. You may ask the keeper."

"I will not."

"No?"

"No." The boy's mouth tightens. "It is not my business. I did not see it." He turns to the fire and sits, stiffly, with his back to the tree, and begins to feed a stick into the flames. "I only wished to say that it is a very fine one."

Feng lets out a slow breath.

Out of the trees comes Jian, wiping his mouth with the back of his hand. He glances at the empty branch. He glances at Zhao Yao's back. His expression does not change by a hair. But Feng, who knows his face, sees the small hard line at the corner of the mouth go slack, and understands that the boy has been standing out of sight the whole time, and has heard the whole thing.

"It will come down for plum," says Jian, to the air.

"Of course," says Feng.

* * *

They enter the upper valley at midday, and the silence breaks.

It is not a sound, at first. It is a motion. Feng sees it from the corner of his eye as the party comes round the shoulder of a ridge and the ground opens ahead: a long wide meadow, white with snow, with the stream winding across it to a stony ford. Something is moving at the far edge of the trees. A great many somethings. A low dun-colored wave, flowing out of the pines and across the open snow, too fast for deer and too dense for foxes.

"Back," says Tan Ruyan.

She has dropped to one knee. Her spear is level. Behind her, Wei Chen has stood, and his hood has fallen back to show a long still face, and his hand rests on the flat bamboo case.

"Stone-boar," he says. "Forty, at the least. Not a herd. A rout."

Feng sees them now. They are low, heavy, gray-bristled beasts, the size of a calf, with tusks like curved daggers, and they are not charging. They are running. Their eyes roll. Foam flies from their jaws. Behind them, in the trees, other shapes are moving: marsh-deer, rock lizards, a pair of the huge pale hares that live in the upper snow. All of them going the same way, down the meadow, toward the ford.

Toward the party.

"They are not hunting us," says Zhao Yao, wildly. "They are fleeing."

"From what?"

Nobody answers. The first of the boars reaches the stream and goes through it in a burst of white water.

"Ford," says Feng. "We hold the ford." He has already drawn. It is the thing he knows, the thing six years of climbing have given him: a narrow place, a wide enemy, and the choice to stand. "Tan. Left bank. Zhao, right. Wei Chen, behind. Jian..."

He looks back.

His brother is standing beside the trees, ten paces away, with his stick in one hand and the other pressed flat to his chest. His face is the color of tallow. His lips are moving.

"Jian!"

"The water," says the boy. He does not look at Feng. He is staring at the stream, at the glassy shallows, at a place in the center where a great flat stone breaks the surface. "There is a hollow under that stone. Wide as a door. Pebble says..." He catches himself. "It is a cavity. If it falls, it will dam the ford."

"How do you know?"

"The stream is wrong there."

It is not an answer. But there is no time for another. The boars are on them.

* * *

It is a short fight, and Feng will remember it all his life as a thing seen through a narrow window.

He does not remember the first boar. He remembers its tusk, which comes at his thigh at the height of the bad leg and is turned by the flat of his sword with a clang like a bell. He remembers the weight of it, a ton of angry bone and muscle, and the way it screamed. He remembers sliding the blade up under the jaw, as Hu taught him, and the hot rush of blood over his wrist.

He remembers the second, and the third.

They do not stop. That is the thing he cannot get past. There is nothing in their eyes. A boar will charge and gore and trample, and a boar will turn aside at a wound, as any beast will. These do not. They come on in a dun flood, over their own dead, with blind white eyes, and the sound of them is a single enormous sob.

To the left, Tan Ruyan fights with the white spear. It moves like a loom. Yellow light flickers from the point and every boar that comes within a pace of her falls with its legs folded, as if the ground had reached up and taken them. To the right, Zhao Yao fights with his teeth set, and his spear is clumsy and desperate and it works. Behind them, Wei Chen has drawn something long and thin from the bamboo case, and he stands on the bank at the center of the line like a man at a loom of his own.

Feng holds the middle.

He holds it for a minute. He holds it for two. His good leg is trembling. The bad one has gone numb. He has lost count of the dead, and he has not been touched, and he begins to believe that it will hold.

Then the scar in his heel catches fire.

It is exactly the pain he knows. A white wire drawn up the back of the ankle, the calf, the thigh. The pain that comes at the fourth breath of every push in every Stillness Chamber. It has never come in a fight. It comes now, all at once, with a violence that bends him double, and he sees his own foot swim and blur in a haze of red.

No. Not now. Not now.

The boar hits him.

* * *

He is on his back in the stream with the sky swinging over him.

He does not know how he got there. There is water in his mouth, and cold on his neck, and something very heavy on his chest that, as he stares, resolves into a boar with its head half off. It is dead. It has been dead for a moment. It lies across him in a spreading cloud of pink.

"Feng!"

He rolls. He gets his hands under the carcass and shoves. It slides away. He sits up in the shallows with his blade still in his fist and his leg a long sheet of white agony, and sees his brother.

Jian is standing in the center of the ford, ankle-deep, ten paces upstream.

He is holding the stick in both hands like a man holding a bar. He is not looking at the boars. He is looking down, at the glassy water, and his lips are drawn back from his teeth, and the pangolin on his collar has all its scales raised.

He brings the stick down on the flat stone.

Feng has never heard a sound like it. It is not a crack. It is a deep, round, ringing note, like a struck bell, and it goes down through the water and the rock and the earth beneath. For the length of a heartbeat the whole ford rings. Then the stone under the water shivers, and splits, and the hollow Jian saw, the cavity wide as a door, collapses inward with a roar.

The stream jumps. A wall of brown water bursts up the channel, tilts, and goes over the boars in a boiling sheet. They scream. They scatter. The dun flood breaks on the new rapids and turns, like a river meeting a dam, and washes sideways into the trees.

Silence. Real silence, this time. The kind with a bottom.

Hollow Echo, Feng thinks. He used it. He has been told to keep it quiet.

There is no Elder within three hundred paces. There is only a ford, and a dead boar, and a boy with a stick, and a brother in the shallows with a leg that will not move.

"Feng," says Jian. He has crossed the water. He is kneeling beside him with his hands out, and there is blood on his face that is not his own. "Where?"

"The heel."

"The old one."

"The old one."

His brother's small cold fingers close on the ankle. They press, gently, along the line of the scar, and Feng bites his tongue to keep from crying out. The pain is a pillar of white. Under it, he can feel the scar pulsing: a thin, hot, regular beat, like a second heart.

"It is reacting," says Jian, very low.

"To what?"

"I do not know." The boy's voice is shaking. "I cannot see. I cannot... Pebble says there is a thread. It is in the water. In the boars. In all of them." He swallows. "It is the same as yours."

In all of them.

Feng looks past his brother's shoulder. The nearest boar lies on its side in the shallows with its legs folded and its jaws agape. Under the stiff gray bristle at its throat, just where the skin folds, a thin black line shows. Not blood. A hair-fine thread, glossy and dry, wound once around the neck and sunk into the flesh.

He has seen it before. He saw it on his own heel when the Healer Song unwound the bandage, and said the words he had been trying not to hear for six years.

Blood hook.

* * *

"It is a thread," he tells them, on the bank.

They have carried him up out of the water. Wei Chen has bound the leg with a strip of indigo cloth and a sliver of jade, and has said that it is not broken, only badly torn. Tan Ruyan sits on a rock a little distance off, wiping her spear. Zhao Yao is shivering in a cloak. Jian has not moved from Feng's side.

"It was set when I was ten," he says. His voice is flat and tired. "I do not remember who. I remember a man with a lamp. He came to the clan hall in the spring, with the Register. He said he was an examiner. He laid his hand on my head, and then on my heel, and said it was a measure of the bones. It hurt." He looks at the water. "I did not think about it again for six years."

"Healer Song says it was cut with an Enforcement Hall blade," says Jian quietly.

"A straight blade. Yes." Feng closes his eyes. "He says the hook was set deep, and then the thread was cut, to leave the barb. It is not a leash. It is a tuning. It makes me hear a certain note." His laugh is short and bitter. "I have been listening to it for six years. I thought it was the pressure. I thought I was weak."

"You are not weak."

"I have a leg that fails at the fourth breath of every Foundation attempt. I have failed it eleven times. I thought it was my fault." He opens his eyes. "It was never my fault. It was the hook. They set it in me so that I would never break through."

Silence on the bank.

"Why?" says Tan Ruyan.

It is the first thing she has said. She has put down her spear. She is looking at him with a clear, grave, unfamiliar face, with none of her smile in it.

"I do not know," says Feng. "Who benefits from a first-ranker who cannot reach Foundation?" He looks at his hands. "I think someone wanted me where I was. On the stair. At the fortieth landing. Climbing. For six years."

At the fortieth landing.

He does not say it. But he feels his brother's hand tighten, very slightly, on his ankle, and knows that the boy has heard.

Tan Ruyan comes and kneels in front of him when the others have turned away.

She does not speak at first. She takes a small flat box of white jade from the satchel at her hip and opens it. Inside is a single dark red pill, glossy as a bead. "Blood Seal," she says. "Level 1, tier low, quality top. Qingshi made. My mother sends me a box each season." She sets it in his palm. "I would rather it were used than kept."

"I cannot pay for it."

"I did not ask you to." Her eyes are level. "Listen. In Qingshi, my father's house trades in many things. A few years ago a man came to the counting-room with a jar of black thread and offered a very good price. My father had him put out. He said that the thing had a smell." She closes Feng's fingers over the pill. "I did not understand that until today. I think you may find, if you look, that a great many families have been offered the same jar."

She stands. She picks up her spear.

"It is not a favor, Senior Brother," she says. "It is information. I find I do not like being the only one who does not know."

Feng swallows the pill. It tastes of salt and iron. The pain in his leg dulls, a little, and the world steadies.

A rival, he thinks. And the first person to say a useful thing all day.

* * *

They find the vine at dusk, and it is already gone.

It lies in a hidden cleft above the upper meadow, behind a screen of frozen waterfall, where the Overseer's map said it would be. The cleft is a small round bowl of rock, thirty paces across, sheltered from the wind, warm as a kitchen. The air is thick and sweet. There is a pool in the center, black as ink, and around the pool, on the ledges and in the cracks, a low green thicket of knotted stems.

Ninefold marrow vine. Level 2. The rarest thing in the valley.

Wei Chen goes in first, with his hand on the bamboo case. He stops at the edge of the pool. For a long moment he does not speak.

"Cut," he says.

Feng, carried on Zhao Yao's shoulder, looks past him. The thicket is not a thicket. It is a ring of stumps, each as thick as a wrist, sliced clean through a hand above the soil. Nine stumps. A tenth, still green and growing, rises beside them. The cut faces are pale, wet and fresh. No more than two days old.

"With a knife," says Wei Chen. "Not iron. Bone. Or glass." He stoops. "A single stroke."

"Who?" says Zhao Yao.

"Someone who knew where to look."

Jian has gone very quiet. He has come to the edge of the pool with his stick, and he stands, with his head tilted, looking at the black water.

"Pebble," he says. His voice is a thread. "There was a thing here."

"What kind of thing?"

"A trail." He crouches. His hand goes down to the damp earth beside the stumps, and comes up with a smear on the fingertips. In the dying light it is dark and glossy and faintly rust-red. "They left it for us."

He holds the hand out. Feng looks at the smear.

It is not blood. It is not mud. It is a brown-black residue, thin as paint, that has set on the skin like the glaze on a pot.

He knows what it is. He has seen it on the Deacon's glass.

Iron ink.

And beside the ring of stumps, pressed into the soft earth of the bank with a firm and careful hand, so that it will not wash away, is a single footprint. A bare foot. Long. Narrow. The toes are very wide apart.

It is not the print of a man. It is the print of something that learned to be one.
